lesson: Re-declaring a schedule under the same id replaces it and says so, which is how a repeating long-horizon task is advanced rather than accumulated: after two declarations one record remains, now due at the later date. The finding is in the first declaration, which reports replaced:true even in a workspace that has never held that id — because a plan with two effects is run three times to collect two approvals, and every already-granted effect is performed again on each pass. A task that blocks does not execute on that run; it executes on the run where its hash is granted, and on every run after it. So the first write here happened twice. There is no way to avoid that by collecting all the hashes first, because a request hash binds the *resolved* input and a later task's input can depend on an earlier task's output, which only exists once that earlier effect has actually run. For long-horizon work that is the property to design around: an effect reached through a multi-grant plan must be idempotent, as replacing a schedule by id is, or it will be performed once per remaining approval. It is also why the mailbox in this repository holds three hundred posts from a round that posts three.
